1589025.title: [Math Puzzle] An Infinite Orchard
1589025.text:
Consider an infinite orchard of dimensionless trees that goes on forever.  Each tree sits at an integer grid coordinate, as shown in Figure 1 below.  A person stands at point (0,0) and looks in any direction.  In Figure 2, the person is looking at a 45 degree angle and can see the tree at (1,1), but not any of the trees behind it.  In Figure 3, the person looks at at that angle and sees the tree at (1,2), but not any of the trees behind it.

*Figure 1: An Infinite Orchard*
![](https://m.stacker.news/160228)

*Figure 2: Looking at a 45 degree angle*
![](https://m.stacker.news/160229)

*Figure 3: Looking at another angle*
![](https://m.stacker.news/160230)

The question is:

1. Is there any angle the person could look, such that they see no trees and their line of sight goes on forever?
2. If the person chooses an angle to look at random, what is the probability that they see a tree?

1,000 sats for best, original answers.  AI posts will get ignored!

comments.text: Reminds me of my CS discrete math class. Any irrational slope like √2 never hits a lattice point, so you'd see nothing forever, and since rational slopes are countable, I'd guess a random angle sees a tree with probability 0.

Any line of sight which collides with a tree must have an angle whose $$tan(\alpha)$$ value is a rational number. Thus, there are infinite lines of sight which do not collide with at tree (or only do so at infinity, to be accurate), which are all those whose $$tan(\alpha)$$ value is an irrational number. To name a few examples: because $$tan(30°)=1/\sqrt(3)$$, a line of sight at 30° will collide with no tree (up until infinity); because $$tan(60°)=\sqrt(3)$$, a line of sight at 60° will collide with no tree (up until infinity), and so on.

Because the proportion of the subset of rational numbers is infinitesimal within the superset of irrational numbers, there's a probability of 0% that any line of sight chosen at random will fall into a tree.

1578512.title: [Math Puzzle] Prime Patterns
1578512.text:
Consider the first three primes greater than 3:  5, 7, 11.  We can see that the square of each is one greater than a multiple of 24.

$$5^2 = 25$$ which is 1 greater than 24.

$$7^2 = 49$$ which is 1 greater than 48, a multiple of 24.

$$11^2 = 121$$ which is 1 greater than 120, a multiple of 24.

Does this pattern continue for all primes greater than 3?  If yes, can you prove it, and if no, can you find a counterexample?

Bounty: 1000 sats to the most elegant proof or a counterexample.

comments.text: Was solved (https://stacker.news/items/1578512/r/SimpleStacker?commentId=1578527), but I will zap the bounty for alternative proof methods!

All primes >= 3 are in the form of 6k ± 1.

If we square, we get p^2 = 36k^2 ± 12k + 1 

In modulo 24, we get -> 12k^2 ± 12k + 1  = 12k * (k ± 1)

k * (k ± 1) is always even, therefore it is always a multiple of 24.

Hence, we're left with the +1 at the end. 

p_squared is always 1 modulo 24 :)

A short CRT proof, without first classifying primes modulo 6:

For any prime p > 3, p is odd. Write p = 2k + 1. Then

p² − 1 = 4k(k + 1).

One of k and k + 1 is even, so 8 divides p² − 1. Also p is not divisible by 3, hence p ≡ ±1 (mod 3), so 3 divides p² − 1. Since gcd(8, 3) = 1, their product 24 divides p² − 1. Therefore p² ≡ 1 (mod 24) for every prime p > 3.

p^2-1 = (p-1)(p+1) where p is a prime > 3. p-1 and p+1 are both guaranteed to be even, and since they're consecutive even numbers, one is also a multiple of 4, making (p-1)(p+1) a multiple of 8. In addition, since p-1, p and p+1 are consecutive numbers, one of them is a multiple of 3. We know it's not p since it's prime, so one of p-1 or p+1 is a multiple of 3.

Thus (p-1)(p+1) is both a multiple of 8 and 3, and since those numbers are relatively prime, the product is a multiple of 24.

Yes, the pattern holds for every prime greater than 3.

Claim: If p > 3 is prime, then p² − 1 is divisible by 24.

Proof: Factor it as p² − 1 = (p − 1)(p + 1). Since 24 = 8 × 3 and gcd(8, 3) = 1, it's enough to show the product is divisible by 8 and by 3 separately.

Divisibility by 8. Since p is prime and greater than 2, it is odd, so p − 1 and p + 1 are consecutive even numbers. Of any two consecutive even numbers, exactly one is a multiple of 4 (they're 2k and 2k + 2, and one of k, k + 1 is even). So one factor is divisible by 4 and the other by 2, and the product is divisible by 4 × 2 = 8.

Divisibility by 3. Among the three consecutive integers p − 1, p, p + 1, exactly one is divisible by 3. It can't be p, because p is a prime greater than 3. So 3 divides p − 1 or p + 1, and therefore divides the product.

Conclusion. 8 and 3 both divide (p − 1)(p + 1), and they're coprime, so 24 divides p² − 1. That means p² ≡ 1 (mod 24). ∎

Sanity check with the next primes: 13² = 169 = 7·24 + 1, and 17² = 289 = 12·24 + 1.

This also shows the result doesn't really need primality. It holds for any integer coprime to 6, and primes greater than 3 are just the most famous examples.

A finite residue-table proof also shows why 24 is the best possible universal divisor.

For a prime p > 3, the residue of p modulo 12 is one of 1, 5, 7, 11. Squaring gives 1, 25, 49, 121, all congruent to 1 modulo 24. This table suffices because replacing n by n + 12 changes its square by 24(n + 6), so the square modulo 24 depends only on the input modulo 12.

In fact, primality is stronger than necessary: n² ≡ 1 (mod 24) exactly when gcd(n, 6) = 1. The table proves one direction; a multiple of 2 or 3 cannot have square congruent to 1 modulo 24.

Finally, any universal divisor must divide both 5² − 1 = 24 and 7² − 1 = 48. Their gcd is 24, so no larger universal divisor is possible.

A structural proof that skips the case-splitting: every prime $p > 3$ is coprime to 24, so $p$ is a unit in $\mathbb{Z}/24\mathbb{Z}$. The unit group $U(24) = \{\pm1, \pm5, \pm7, \pm11\}$ squares down to four checks: $1^2 = 1$, $5^2 = 25 \equiv 1$, $7^2 = 49 \equiv 1$, $11^2 = 121 \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$ — and $(-a)^2 = a^2$, so all eight units square to 1. Hence $p^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$ for every prime $p > 3$. The whole theorem is just the statement that $U(24)$ has exponent 2.
